items.stem: What fundamentally flows between cmdlets in a PowerShell pipeline?

options.rationale: Correct: PowerShell passes rich objects, so downstream cmdlets can select and filter by property.
Traditional shells pass text; PowerShell passes objects.
File handles are not what the pipeline carries.
The pipeline carries data objects, not executables.

items.explanation: Correct: PowerShell passes rich objects, so downstream cmdlets can select and filter by property.

items.stem: Which statements about error handling in PowerShell are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: try/catch reliably catches a non-terminating error only if you add -ErrorAction Stop
options.rationale: Correct: non-terminating errors must be escalated to terminating with -ErrorAction Stop (or $ErrorActionPreference) to be caught.

options.text: A terminating error stops the current pipeline and can be caught by catch
options.rationale: Correct: terminating errors transfer control to the catch block.

options.text: catch blocks run even when no error occurred
options.rationale: catch runs only when a terminating error is thrown in the try block.
Write-Error produces a non-terminating error by default and does not stop the script.

items.explanation: Correct: non-terminating errors must be escalated to terminating with -ErrorAction Stop (or $ErrorActionPreference) to be caught.; Correct: terminating errors transfer control to the catch block.

items.stem: By default, how does the -eq comparison operator treat letter case for strings?

options.rationale: Correct: -eq is case-insensitive by default; use -ceq for a case-sensitive comparison.
That is -ceq; the plain -eq ignores case.

options.text: It throws an error on strings
It only compares the first character

items.explanation: Correct: -eq is case-insensitive by default; use -ceq for a case-sensitive comparison.
